paragraphs.text: We work in the thin-lens, paraxial approximation, with the same homogeneous medium on both sides of the lens.
The formula relates three quantities: the object-to-lens distance $d$, the image-to-lens distance $f$, and the focal length $F$.

The lowercase letter denotes image distance and the uppercase letter denotes focal length;
their sign convention is stated below.
We first derive the formula from the converging-lens construction of a real image in Figure 179, with the object beyond the object-side focus.

Both foci have the same letter in the figure;
each triangle below uses the focus on its own side. This construction does not represent every signed imaging case.

The triangles $\triangle ABF$ and $\triangle DOF$ are similar, so:
$\frac{\lvert OD\rvert}{\lvert AB\rvert}=\frac{\lvert OF\rvert}{\lvert BF\rvert}$

Since $\lvert OD\rvert=\lvert A_1B_1\rvert$, we obtain:
$\frac{\lvert A_1B_1\rvert}{\lvert AB\rvert}=\frac{\lvert OF\rvert}{\lvert BF\rvert}=\frac{F}{d-F}$ (6.15)

Likewise, $\triangle COF$ and $\triangle A_1B_1F$ are similar, giving:
$\frac{\lvert A_1B_1\rvert}{\lvert OC\rvert}=\frac{\lvert B_1F\rvert}{\lvert OF\rvert}$

Using $\lvert OC\rvert=\lvert AB\rvert$, we get:
$\frac{\lvert A_1B_1\rvert}{\lvert AB\rvert}=\frac{f-F}{F}$ (6.16)
Equating the right-hand sides of (6.15) and (6.16):
$\frac{F}{d-F}=\frac{f-F}{F}$

Hence:
$F^2=fd-fF-Fd+F^2$
Or $fF+Fd=fd$.

The denominators and distance product are nonzero in this construction. Dividing each term by $Ffd$ gives:
$\frac{1}{d}+\frac{1}{f}=\frac{1}{F}$ (6.17)

In terms of the optical power of the lens, this is:
$\frac{1}{d}+\frac{1}{f}=D$ (6.18)
We use the convention that real objects, real images, and real focal lengths are positive. The formula also applies to virtual objects, virtual images, and diverging lenses;

the sign convention is stated here without a further proof.
A converging lens has a real focus, so the $\frac{1}{|F|}$ term has a positive sign.

For a diverging lens, $F<0$, and the right-hand side of (6.17) is $-\frac{1}{|F|}$.
The $\frac{1}{|f|}$ term is positive for a real image and negative for a virtual image.

The $\frac{1}{|d|}$ term is positive for a real luminous object;
the $\frac{1}{|d|}$ term is negative for a virtual object.
A virtual object is the point that incoming converging rays would reach if continued in their incident directions without being changed by the lens. It is not an actual light source at that position.
When $F$, $f$, or $d$ is unknown, retain the signed unknown in $\frac{1}{F}$, $\frac{1}{f}$, or $\frac{1}{d}$, with a positive coefficient in front of the term.
This notation does not assume that the unknown value is positive, and a guessed sign must not be applied a second time.
A negative result for the focal length, image distance, or object distance indicates a virtual focus, virtual image, or virtual object, respectively, in this convention.

**Lens Magnification**
The image formed by a lens generally differs in size from the object. Magnification describes this size relationship.

**Linear magnification is the ratio of an image linear size to the corresponding object linear size.**
These are size magnitudes;
their signs are not used to describe upright or inverted orientation.

Returning to Figure 179, let the height of the object $AB$ be $h$ and the height of the image $A_1B_1$ be $H$.
The linear magnification is:
$\Gamma=\frac{H}{h}$
Both heights are nonnegative size magnitudes, and the object height is nonzero.

The triangles $\triangle OAB$ and $\triangle OA_1B_1$ are similar, so the ratio of corresponding lengths gives:
$\frac{H}{h}=\frac{|f|}{|d|}$
Absolute values are used for image and object distances because this is a ratio of sizes.
upright or inverted orientation must be determined separately from the image construction.
